Knowledge is the state of genuinely holding something true in your mind, with good reason to believe it. When you say you know something, you're claiming more than guessing or feeling — you're saying that what you hold in your mind correctly reflects reality, and that you have a solid basis for holding it.
The Classic Definition: Justified True Belief

For centuries, the most widely accepted definition of knowledge is justified true belief. This means three things must all be true at once:

1. It must be true. You cannot know something false. If someone in ancient times "knew" that the Sun revolves around the Earth, they did not actually have knowledge — they had a false belief. Truth is non-negotiable for knowledge.

2. You must believe it. A fact sitting in an unread book isn't anyone's knowledge. You have to genuinely hold something as true in your mind for it to be your knowledge.

3. You must have justification. If you guess that it will rain tomorrow and it does rain, you were right — but you didn't know it would rain. Justification means you have good reason, evidence, or a reliable basis for your belief. A lucky guess doesn't count.

Put simply: Knowledge = a true belief that you have good reason to hold.
A Famous Challenge: The Gettier Problem

In 1963, philosopher Edmund Gettier showed that meeting all three conditions might still not be enough to guarantee knowledge. His examples involve situations where someone has a justified true belief, but only by coincidence — and we'd hesitate to call that knowledge.

A simple version: imagine you glance at a clock on the wall. It reads 3:00. Your belief is true — it really is 3:00. And you're justified in trusting the clock. But unknown to you, the clock stopped exactly 12 hours ago. You happened to look at it at the right moment. You got lucky. Did you know it was 3:00?

Most people feel the answer is no — and this is the Gettier problem. It shows that knowledge is slightly more elusive than the three-part definition suggests. Philosophers have proposed many fixes, but there's still no universal agreement on the perfect definition. For everyday and practical purposes, justified true belief remains the most useful and widely used starting point.

Knowledge isn't one single thing — it comes in meaningfully different forms.

1. Knowing that — Propositional Knowledge

This is knowledge of facts. It takes the form "I know that...":

  • "I know that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen."
  • "I know that India became independent in 1947."

These are statements that are either true or false, and when you know them, you hold the true ones correctly. This is the type of knowledge most discussed in education and intellectual life.

2. Knowing how — Procedural Knowledge

This is knowledge of how to do something. "I know how to swim." "I know how to ride a bicycle." You might be able to do something skillfully without being able to explain it in words. A skilled musician might not be able to describe how their fingers find the right notes — but they know how. This kind of knowledge lives in practice, habit, and the body, not just in language and facts.

3. Knowing of — Acquaintance Knowledge

This is knowing something through direct experience or personal familiarity. "I know Paris" — meaning you've been there, you've walked its streets. "I know her" — meaning you've met and interacted with her. You can know hundreds of facts about Paris without ever having visited — but in this sense, you don't "know Paris." Acquaintance knowledge comes from direct, first-hand contact.
How Knowledge Differs from Closely Related Words

This is where understanding the word "knowledge" gets sharper.

Knowledge vs. Information
Information is raw data or facts that exist in the world — in books, databases, or on the internet. Knowledge is what happens when that information is genuinely grasped by a mind. A library holds vast information, but the library itself knows nothing. Knowledge requires a knower.

Knowledge vs. Belief
A belief is anything you accept as true in your mind — but beliefs can be false. You might firmly believe something incorrect. Knowledge requires the belief to actually be true and to be justified. All knowledge involves belief, but not all belief is knowledge. Knowledge is a specific, qualified kind of belief.

Knowledge vs. Opinion
An opinion is a view you hold, especially on matters involving judgment, values, or interpretation. Opinions can be thoughtful or shallow, well-supported or poorly supported. But even a carefully held opinion on a genuinely contested question isn't usually called "knowledge" — knowledge implies a higher degree of certainty and a firmer factual basis.

Knowledge vs. Understanding
Understanding goes deeper than knowledge. To know something is to hold a fact correctly. To understand it is to grasp why it's true, how it connects to other things, and to see the bigger picture. You might know that mixing an acid and a base produces a neutralization reaction — but understanding chemistry means grasping the mechanism, the patterns, the implications. Knowledge is a building block; understanding is what you build with it. You can have knowledge without understanding, but you cannot have deep understanding without knowledge.

Knowledge vs. Wisdom
Wisdom is the ability to use knowledge and understanding well — to make sound judgments, act appropriately, and know what truly matters in a given situation. Wisdom is the mature, lived application of knowledge over time and experience. A person can accumulate enormous knowledge and still act foolishly. And wisdom often includes knowing the limits of one's own knowledge — knowing what you don't know. You can have knowledge without wisdom, but wisdom almost always contains knowledge.

Knowledge reaches us through several distinct pathways:

Experience and perception. We see, hear, touch, smell, and interact with the world around us, and we learn from it directly. This is the most fundamental and immediate source of knowledge.

Reasoning. By thinking carefully and drawing logical conclusions from what we already know, we can arrive at new knowledge — including about things we have never directly observed. Mathematics and logic are prime examples.

Testimony. Much of what we know, we were told — by teachers, books, trusted people, or reliable institutions. We take on their knowledge by trusting their credibility. Most of your knowledge about history, science, and the world at large came through testimony.

Memory. Knowledge gained in the past must be stored and recalled to remain useful. Without memory, every moment would begin from zero.

Introspection. We can know things about our own inner life — our thoughts, feelings, sensations, and desires — in a way no one else can access directly. You know you're in pain; you know you're feeling happy. This is knowledge of yourself from the inside.

Knowledge has real boundaries, and recognizing them is a mark of intellectual honesty.

There are things that are currently unknown — humanity hasn't figured them out yet. There are things that may be unknowable in principle — questions where no amount of evidence or reasoning can fully settle the matter. There are also things we think we know but are actually wrong about — confident false belief that masquerades as knowledge.

Acknowledging what you don't know is not a weakness; it is the very foundation of honest thinking, good science, and continued learning. The philosopher Socrates famously said that true wisdom begins with knowing the limits of one's own knowledge.

Knowledge can belong to a single person, or it can be held collectively. A doctor has medical knowledge. A culture carries knowledge passed down through generations — stories, practices, observations about the world. Libraries, universities, and scientific institutions exist to preserve, verify, and transmit the collective knowledge of humanity across time.

When someone says "we know" — as in "we know the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old" — they mean that this is part of humanity's collective body of verified knowledge, even if any single person hasn't personally checked every piece of evidence.

Knowledge is a true belief that you are justified in holding. It is more than a guess, more than an opinion, and more than mere information — it requires truth, belief, and justification together. It comes in factual, practical, and experiential forms. It is deeper than information, less complete than understanding, and the foundation of wisdom. It enters the mind through experience, reasoning, testimony, memory, and introspection. And it has genuine limits — which honest thinkers embrace rather than ignore.
